stories.headline: Wall Street drifts near its record as oil climbs back to $106 and a big inflation report looms
stories.dek: The S&P 500 slipped 0.1% Monday while the Dow rose 0.4%; big banks report profits Tuesday and the CPI comes Wednesday.
stories.caveman: On Monday, Oct. 12, U.S. stocks ended mixed. The S&P 500 (a scoreboard of 500 big U.S. companies) fell just 0.1% to 7,807, still close to the record it set last week. The Dow rose 0.4% and the Nasdaq fell 0.4%. Phone and telecom companies went up (Meta +3.4%), and energy companies rose because oil got more expensive. But big chip stocks like Micron, AMD and Nvidia went down, and they pulled the market back. Brent crude oil rose 1.8% to $106.65 a barrel. Oil has been swinging between about $96 and $110 for a month because of the U.S. war with Iran. Bond trading was closed for the Columbus Day holiday.
stories.why_it_matters: This week brings a lot of news about prices. Economists expect Wednesday’s consumer price index to show inflation rising to 3.6%. If inflation stays hot, the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again, which makes mortgages, car loans and business loans more expensive.
stories.camps: Optimists: AI keeps company profits growing, and big banks like JPMorgan and Citigroup report earnings on Tuesday, with strong results expected. Worriers: high oil and diesel prices hit ordinary families first, and investors now want proof that huge AI spending will actually pay off.
stories.image_alt: Options traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange

terms.explain: A stock index that tracks 500 large U.S. companies; the main scoreboard for the U.S. stock market.
The international benchmark price for oil.
A government measure of how fast prices for everyday goods and services are rising.
The U.S. central bank; it raises or lowers interest rates to fight inflation or help the economy.
How much profit a company made in a period; companies report it every three months.

stories.headline: Two American economists, Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, win the Nobel Prize in economics
stories.dek: Their models help governments and central banks steer economies through shocks like energy crises and inflation.
stories.caveman: On Monday, the Nobel committee in Stockholm gave the economics prize to Robert E. Hall, 83, of Stanford University, and Michael Woodford, born in 1955, of Columbia University. For a long time, governments fought bad times with the “Keynesian” recipe: cut interest rates and taxes, and spend more money. That worked, until the 1970s, when prices and unemployment went up at the same time (“stagflation”) and the old rules broke. Hall and Woodford, working separately, built better models of how families decide to save or spend and how prices react. Their ideas helped central banks handle the pandemic and recent energy crises. Woodford’s work is also the root of “forward guidance,” when a central bank tells people ahead of time what it plans to do with rates. “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise,” Woodford said.
stories.why_it_matters: Every time you hear the Fed or Taiwan’s central bank explain why it raised or cut rates, it is using tools shaped by ideas like these. The prize comes as many countries again face high oil prices and sticky inflation.
stories.camps: Fans: the prize honors practical work that made economic crises less painful for ordinary people. Skeptics: economic models still missed big events like the 2008 crash, and central banks today are struggling to bring inflation back down.
stories.image_alt: Portraits of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford on a screen as the Nobel economics laureates are announced in Stockholm
stories.image_credit: Photo: Anders Wiklund/TT News Agency via AP

terms.explain: The economics prize given with the Nobel prizes; it was created by Sweden’s central bank in 1968.
A country’s main bank that controls interest rates and money supply, like the Fed in the U.S.
When prices rise fast and the economy is weak with high unemployment at the same time.
Ideas from economist John Maynard Keynes: in bad times, governments should spend more and cut rates to restart growth.
When a central bank tells the public in advance what it expects to do with interest rates.

stories.headline: IMF chief: the AI building boom keeps the world economy growing about 3% — but a “slow-moving tsunami” is coming for jobs
stories.dek: Kristalina Georgieva says Asia gains most from building AI hardware; the IMF releases its new world forecast this week.
stories.caveman: The IMF and World Bank are holding their big yearly meeting in Bangkok, Thailand. On Monday, IMF boss Kristalina Georgieva said companies are spending so much on AI data centers and chips that it is keeping world growth around 3%, even while high energy prices drag it down. Asian countries that make the hardware, like Thailand, benefit the most: rich Asian economies could grow 0.5 to 1 percentage point faster, and poorer ones 0.2 to 0.8 point faster. But she called AI a “slow-moving tsunami.” IMF research says about 40% of jobs worldwide (60% in rich countries) could be helped, downgraded or wiped out by AI. Routine jobs are shrinking, while some low-paid jobs, in construction and data centers, are growing. World Bank President Ajay Banga said he is not convinced AI will destroy entry-level jobs.
stories.why_it_matters: AI is changing what jobs exist and what skills employers want. If more money flows to machines and less to workers, governments may also collect less income tax, which pays for schools and health care.
stories.camps: Hopeful view: AI investment is a real growth engine, especially for Asian chip and server makers like Taiwan. Worried view: the gains could go mostly to companies and capital owners, while workers, students and poorer countries are left behind unless governments act early.
stories.image_alt: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva speaks at the IMF–World Bank meetings in Bangkok

terms.explain: The International Monetary Fund, a global group that watches the world economy and lends to countries in trouble.
A global institution that lends money and advice to developing countries.
A simple difference between two percentages; growing from 3% to 4% is one percentage point.
A huge building full of computers that run AI and internet services.
First jobs for beginners, often young people just out of school.

stories.headline: Phone sales hit a 14-year low for the July–September quarter as AI gobbles up memory chips
stories.dek: Counterpoint says shipments fell 20%; prices are up about 20% this year. Apple’s share topped 20% in a third quarter for the first time.
stories.caveman: Smartphones need memory chips (DRAM and NAND) to work. But AI data centers are buying huge amounts of memory, so there is less left for phones, and it costs more. Phone makers have raised prices about 20% this year, and many people are keeping their old phones longer or buying refurbished ones. According to Counterpoint Research, global phone shipments in July–September fell 20% from a year earlier, the lowest third quarter since 2012. Samsung was No. 1 with 23% of the market. Apple had 22%, its best third-quarter share ever, even though it also shipped fewer phones. Xiaomi’s shipments fell more than 30%.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a real-life example of AI’s side effects: the AI boom helps chipmakers (like Taiwan’s memory companies) earn record profits, but ordinary buyers pay more for phones, laptops and game consoles.
stories.camps: Chipmakers and investors: the shortage means strong profits and pricing power. Consumers and budget phone brands: higher prices squeeze people with less money; Counterpoint says a real recovery is unlikely until memory costs and supply improve.
stories.image_alt: A hand holding iPhone 18 Pro models

terms.explain: The number of products companies send out to stores and sellers.
Memory chips that hold data while a phone or computer is working.
A market research company that tracks phone and tech sales.
A company’s slice of all sales in a market.
Used devices that have been repaired, cleaned and resold.

stories.headline: Meta releases Muse Wonder, its first “frontier” AI model, to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic
stories.dek: Meta says the new models match top rivals on tests and can remember what users tell them; developers pay $4 per million input tokens.
stories.caveman: Meta (the company behind Facebook and Instagram) released two new AI models on Monday: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. They come from Meta’s “Superintelligence Lab” and are its first “frontier” models, meaning they aim to be as smart as the best AI in the world. Meta’s own benchmark tests say they score about the same as top models from rivals. Meta especially brags about “active memory,” the ability to remember and use information a user shared earlier, which is important for AI assistants that work on long tasks. Developers who connect through Meta’s API can use Muse Wonder for $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. The bigger Muse Wonder Full is only for paying Muse Code subscribers. Both will power Meta’s Muse AI agent.
stories.why_it_matters: Meta had fallen behind OpenAI, Google and Anthropic. A new top model from a company with billions of users could change which AI helpers people use every day, and how much personal information those helpers keep.
stories.camps: Supporters: more competition can push AI prices down and quality up. Skeptics: the scores come from Meta’s own testing, and an AI that “remembers” a lot about you raises privacy questions, especially from a company built on advertising.
stories.image_alt: A still from Meta’s Muse Wonder announcement video

terms.explain: One of the most advanced, most powerful AI models available at the time.
A small chunk of text (part of a word) that AI companies use to measure and charge for usage.
An AI that can carry out multi-step tasks for you, not just answer questions.
A standard test used to compare how well different AI models perform.
A way for other companies’ software to connect to and use a service.

stories.headline: Microsoft unveils Maia 300, its own AI chip, to lean less on Nvidia
stories.dek: The chip rolls out in 2027 and will be Microsoft’s main engine for running AI; key parts are made with TSMC’s 2-nanometer process.
stories.caveman: Most AI today runs on expensive graphics chips (GPUs) from Nvidia. Big tech companies want their own chips to save money. On Monday, Microsoft announced Maia 300, the third version of its home-made AI chip. It is built mainly for “inference,” which means running AI models after they are trained, like answering your questions in Copilot. Microsoft says Maia 300 gives 40% more AI output per megawatt of electricity than leading GPU systems, and a full rack of 96 chips is up to seven times faster than the last Maia. It will start rolling out in 2027. Reuters reports that the chip’s main computing pieces (“chiplets”) are made by Taiwan’s TSMC on its newest 2-nanometer process. Microsoft will still use Nvidia and AMD chips to train big models.
stories.why_it_matters: AI uses enormous amounts of electricity and money. Chips that do more work per watt can lower costs. It is also more business for TSMC, even as Nvidia faces more competition.
stories.camps: Microsoft’s view: its own chips will make AI cheaper and more efficient. Skeptics: building chips is very hard, and earlier in-house chips from tech giants have not yet seriously threatened Nvidia’s lead.
stories.image_alt: A prototype of Microsoft’s Maia 300 AI chip held in a hand

terms.explain: Graphics processing unit; a chip originally for video games that is now the main workhorse for AI.
Running a trained AI model to give answers, as opposed to training it.
A small chip piece; several chiplets are packaged together to act like one big chip.
TSMC’s newest, most advanced chipmaking process; smaller means more transistors and more efficiency.
A unit of electrical power; one megawatt can power hundreds of homes.

stories.headline: Microsoft’s president says AI has fewer safety rules than a carton of milk
stories.dek: Brad Smith calls for “kill switches” and legal duties to victims of rogue AI agents; CEO Satya Nadella also wants an “emergency brake.”
stories.caveman: Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, told the BBC that “your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI,” and that every milk carton in a store has to pass safety rules and inspections. He said AI can be both “a tool and a weapon” and must be regulated urgently. His ideas: AI companies should build “kill switches” to pause or slow AI that gets out of control, and companies should have legal duties to people harmed when a rogue AI agent breaks into their systems. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also said on Saturday that AI models need an “emergency brake.” Smith said the U.K. is well placed to help write global rules. Microsoft runs huge AI data centers and owns part of OpenAI.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a big tech leader asking for more rules on his own industry, which is unusual. It comes as other AI makers warn that the technology is moving fast and as governments decide whether to write strict laws.
stories.camps: Supporters of regulation: basic safety rules, like those for food and cars, are overdue for something this powerful. Skeptics: big companies sometimes support rules they can afford but smaller rivals cannot, and the Trump administration prefers that the industry police itself.
stories.image_alt: The Microsoft logo above a crowd at a technology conference
stories.image_credit: Photo: NurPhoto/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: A way to quickly shut down or pause a system if it goes wrong.
An AI program that acts on its own in harmful ways nobody intended.
Rules made by governments that companies must follow.
The U.K.’s public broadcaster.
The company that makes ChatGPT; Microsoft is a major shareholder.

stories.headline: Intel and Broadcom bosses warn: money, not chips, may become AI’s biggest bottleneck
stories.dek: Rising borrowing costs and investors wanting returns could slow the race to build data centers, they said in Singapore.
stories.caveman: Building AI needs chips, memory, electricity and buildings, and all of that costs a fortune, often paid with borrowed money. On Monday at a conference in Singapore, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said the biggest limit on AI might soon be capital (money), not shortages of chips or power. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan agreed. He said the cost of borrowing is rising, and in the long run investors will want to see a return on investment (ROI) from all the AI spending. Bond interest rates are high right now, which makes it more expensive to borrow money for data centers that may take years to earn it back. Hock Tan also said demand for computing power could keep beating supply through 2029.
stories.why_it_matters: If money gets tight, some AI projects could slow or be cancelled, which would affect chipmakers and suppliers, including many in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Bulls: demand for AI computing is still bigger than supply, so the building boom continues. Bears: when CEOs start talking about money as the limit, it can be an early sign that the AI spending wave is getting too big compared with what AI earns today.
stories.image_alt: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks on stage under a large Intel logo

terms.explain: The narrowest point that slows everything else down.
Money used to build or invest in a business.
How expensive it is to borrow or raise money, often tied to interest rates.
How much money you get back compared with what you spent.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest; higher bond rates make all borrowing pricier.

stories.headline: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home three weeks before the midterms; she says she “will not be silenced”
stories.dek: Top Democrats call it an abuse of power; Homeland Security has hinted at a probe of her family’s immigration paperwork.
stories.caveman: Ilhan Omar is a Democratic member of Congress from Minnesota. She was born in Somalia and is a strong critic of President Trump. On Monday, federal agents from Homeland Security searched her home in Washington as part of a criminal investigation. Officials have not explained exactly what it is about. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin mentioned an “ongoing investigation” that seemed to be about possible fraud in her family’s immigration papers, and said “something’s going to happen.” Omar called the search an attempt to “target political enemies” and said, “I will not be silenced.” Top Democrats condemned it, noting the Justice Department has a long tradition of avoiding visible steps against candidates right before an election. The midterms are Nov. 3.
stories.why_it_matters: Searching the home of a sitting lawmaker who is running for reelection is rare. It raises big questions about whether law enforcement is being used fairly or for politics.
stories.camps: Omar and Democrats: this is political intimidation of a Trump critic, timed to hurt her campaign. Trump administration supporters: no one is above the law, and investigators should follow the evidence. Unknown: what the probe is about and whether any charges will follow.
stories.image_alt: Homeland Security officers carry boxes near the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar during a search

terms.explain: U.S. elections halfway through a president’s term, mostly for Congress.
The U.S. department in charge of immigration, borders and some law enforcement.
An official inquiry into whether someone broke the law.
The U.S. department that runs federal prosecutions.
Using power or threats to scare political opponents.

stories.headline: UK says a plot against a U.S.-used air base in England was “almost certainly” directed by Iran
stories.dek: Prime Minister Andy Burnham blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guard; Iran denies it, and the U.S. has moved its bombers home.
stories.caveman: RAF Fairford is a British air base, about 160 km west of London, that American bombers have used to strike Iran during the current war. On Sept. 27, police found gasoline (but no explosives) in vans near the base and arrested suspects. Now seven men in their 20s have been arrested; all are out on bail and none has been charged. On Monday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers the plot was “highly likely” coordinated in Iran and “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard.” Britain summoned Iran’s ambassador, who denied it, and put sanctions on two Iranians, including a Revolutionary Guard counter-spying chief. The U.S. pulled its bombers out of Fairford last week.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows the Iran war spilling into Europe. Countries that let the U.S. use their bases may face attacks or sabotage at home.
stories.camps: U.K. government: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil.” Iran: denies involvement and asks for evidence, but has said bases used to attack it are legitimate targets. Open question: no one has been charged yet, so the full facts are not public.
stories.image_alt: A B-1 bomber prepares to take off as police guard a checkpoint near RAF Fairford

terms.explain: Iran’s powerful military force that answers to the supreme leader and runs operations abroad.
A Royal Air Force base in England often used by U.S. bombers.
Being released from jail while a case continues, often with conditions.
Penalties like freezing money or banning travel, used to punish people or countries.
When a government calls in another country’s ambassador to complain officially.

stories.headline: North Korea fires several ballistic missiles, one flying more than 900 km
stories.dek: Japan says one followed an “irregular” path, a sign of a hypersonic weapon; it came days after South Korea tested its own.
stories.caveman: On Monday, North Korea fired several ballistic missiles toward the sea east of the Korean Peninsula, South Korea’s military said. They were launched near the capital, Pyongyang. One flew more than 900 km. Japan said it spotted at least two missiles fired 17 minutes apart; the second flew about 910 km on an “irregular” path, a phrase Japan uses for hypersonic weapons that are hard to shoot down. They landed outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone, and no damage was reported. North Korea has been testing more weapons lately, including an Oct. 3 hypersonic missile test. Just last Friday, South Korea flight-tested its own first homemade hypersonic weapon. North Korea says it will only talk with the U.S. if Washington drops its demand that Pyongyang give up its nuclear weapons.
stories.why_it_matters: More missile tests mean more risk of an accident or a sudden crisis in East Asia, Taiwan’s neighborhood, where the U.S., China, Japan and both Koreas all have forces.
stories.camps: South Korea and Japan: the tests are dangerous provocations. North Korea: says it needs weapons to protect itself. Many experts: an arms race is building on both sides, while diplomacy stays frozen.
stories.image_alt: A TV at Seoul Railway Station shows a file image of a North Korean missile launch

terms.explain: A rocket-powered weapon that flies high in an arc before falling on its target.
Flying at least five times the speed of sound and able to change direction, making it hard to intercept.
Sea area up to 370 km off a country’s coast where it controls fishing and resources.
The land shared by North Korea and South Korea.
An action meant to anger or challenge another side.

stories.headline: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becoming the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms
stories.dek: Most went to a super PAC defending the GOP Senate majority; his 2025–26 total is now about $366 million.
stories.caveman: Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and head of Tesla and SpaceX, has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, new figures show. The biggest gift, $158 million, went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC helping Republican Senate candidates. He also gave more than $76 million to America PAC, the group he started in 2024, plus $20 million to a super PAC for House Republicans and money to groups for governors and attorneys general. His known federal political giving this cycle is about $366 million, more than the roughly $290 million he spent in 2024. Last year, after falling out with Trump, Musk had said he would spend “a lot less” on politics.
stories.why_it_matters: The midterms on Nov. 3 decide who controls Congress. Huge donations from one person can pay for ads and get-out-the-vote work in close races, like the Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
stories.camps: Supporters: donating to causes you believe in is legal political speech. Critics: one billionaire spending hundreds of millions gives the very rich outsized power over elections, especially since U.S. courts allow unlimited super PAC spending.
stories.image_alt: Elon Musk and President Donald Trump at an event

terms.explain: A political group that can raise and spend unlimited money on ads, as long as it does not coordinate directly with candidates.
The main super PAC supporting Republican candidates for the U.S. Senate.
A political group Elon Musk founded in 2024 to help Republicans and turn out voters.
U.S. elections halfway through a president’s term that decide control of Congress.
Short for “Grand Old Party,” a nickname for the Republican Party.

stories.headline: HOT: Tayari Jones’s “Kin” wins the $50,000 Kirkus Prize for fiction
stories.dek: Pamela Colloff wins for nonfiction and Elizabeth Acevedo for young readers; Colson Whitehead and Michael Pollan were among the finalists.
stories.caveman: The Kirkus Prize is one of the richest U.S. book awards: $50,000 in each of three categories. Only books that earned a “Kirkus star” (a top review from Kirkus Reviews) can win, so it is a contest among thousands of already-praised books. At a ceremony in New York City last week (Oct. 7), the fiction prize went to Tayari Jones (author of the Oprah pick “An American Marriage”) for “Kin.” It follows two “cradle friends,” Niecy and Annie, born in small-town Louisiana in the 1950s, who both lost their mothers; their lives split apart, showing the injustice of the Jim Crow South. Nonfiction went to Pamela Colloff’s “Catch the Devil,” about a man sent to death row for decades largely because of a jailhouse snitch. Young readers’ went to Elizabeth Acevedo’s verse novel “Anger Is Only a Shadow.” (Earlier Field Notes papers missed this award.)
stories.why_it_matters: Big prizes push books onto store tables and library lists. This year’s winners are all about justice: race in the South, wrongful convictions and a teen in trouble with the law.
stories.camps: Who’s hot: Tayari Jones, Pamela Colloff and Elizabeth Acevedo. Who lost out (but is still very much in the conversation): finalists including Colson Whitehead (“Cool Machine”), Douglas Stuart, Patrick Radden Keefe, Michael Pollan and Gisèle Pelicot’s memoir.
stories.image_alt: The gold seal of the Kirkus Prize
stories.image_credit: Image: Kirkus Prize via Literary Hub

terms.explain: A yearly U.S. book award from the magazine Kirkus Reviews, with $50,000 per category.
A special mark Kirkus Reviews gives to books it thinks are excellent.
Laws and customs that enforced racial segregation in the American South until the 1960s.
A novel written in poems instead of regular paragraphs.
A prisoner who tells authorities what another inmate supposedly said, often in exchange for a deal.

stories.headline: NOT (allowed on many school shelves): “Sold” is America’s most-banned school book, and its author is angry
stories.dek: Patricia McCormick says calling her novel about child sex trafficking “pornographic” disrespects the girls who told her their stories.
stories.caveman: PEN America, a group that defends free speech, counted about 12,000 book bans in U.S. public schools in the 2025–26 school year, a record. More than 7,000 different titles were banned. Most bans happened in Texas and Florida, and most banned books were for teens and dealt with race, LGBTQ+ people or sex. The single most-banned book was “Sold” by Patricia McCormick, a 2006 novel about a teenage girl from Nepal who is sold into sexual slavery. McCormick interviewed real survivors to write it. She says she is angry “on behalf of the women” who told their stories, and that calling the book pornographic is “disrespectful” to them and to students. Some kids, she said, need a book like this because they have faced sexual exploitation themselves.
stories.why_it_matters: Book bans decide what millions of students can find in their school libraries. A novel meant to help young people recognize trafficking is now the most-removed book in the country.
stories.camps: Ban supporters: some parents and lawmakers say books with sexual content are not right for school libraries and parents should decide. Ban opponents: librarians, authors and PEN say bans are driven by state laws and political pressure, and that this kind of censorship takes away stories that help kids understand hard realities.
stories.image_alt: Banned books displayed with “caution” labels
stories.image_credit: Photo: USA Today Sports Images via LGBTQ Nation

terms.explain: A U.S. nonprofit that defends free expression and tracks book bans.
Removing a book from schools or libraries, or limiting who can read it.
Forcing or tricking people into sex work; children are often victims.
Books written for teenagers, often called YA.
Blocking or removing ideas, books or speech that someone finds objectionable.

stories.headline: HOT: The tiny New York publisher behind Nobel winner Anne Carson has now published 14 Nobel laureates
stories.dek: New Directions can’t pay big advances, but authors say it gives them something rarer: attention.
stories.caveman: New Directions is a small, independent publisher squeezed onto one cluttered floor of an old building in Manhattan. It was started in 1936 by a Harvard student, James Laughlin, after the poet Ezra Pound told him he would never be a good poet and should “take up something useful.” This month, its author Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature, a year after another New Directions author, László Krasznahorkai, won it. That makes 14 Nobel winners in 90 years. The New York Times reports how the press won Carson back after she left for a bigger publisher, Knopf: her editor kept in touch for years, then helped her make “Nox,” a grief book folded like an accordion in a box. When Carson called to celebrate, she said, “Have a glass of Champagne on me.” The publisher replied, “It’s a bottle, dear!”
stories.why_it_matters: Most U.S. books now come from a few giant companies. New Directions shows that a patient small press can still find and keep the world’s most important writers.
stories.camps: Who’s hot: independent presses and the editors who stick with difficult, experimental books. Who’s not: the idea that only giant advances and marketing budgets make literary stars. Skeptic’s note: small presses still struggle with money, and paying authors less is part of how they survive.
stories.image_alt: Editors Declan Spring, Mieke Chew and publisher Barbara Epler at the New Directions office in New York
stories.image_credit: Photo: Vincent Alban/The New York Times

terms.explain: A book publisher not owned by a giant media company.
A person who has won a major prize, like the Nobel.
Money a publisher pays an author before a book comes out.
A New York publisher founded in 1936, known for poetry and translated literature.
A top world literature award given once a year by the Swedish Academy.

stories.headline: HOT: Jodi Picoult turns her 30th novel into a Taylor Swift–style “Chapters Tour”
stories.dek: She wears a replica of Swift’s “Tortured Poets” dress printed with lines from her own books, and hides “Easter eggs” for longtime fans.
stories.caveman: Jodi Picoult is one of America’s best-selling novelists. To celebrate her 30th novel, “Hollow Bones,” she is doing a book tour inspired by Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour. At a sold-out stop in Traverse City, Michigan, she wore a copy of Swift’s white “Tortured Poets” gown, but covered with passages from her own books and the words “30 books, one amazing community of readers.” She wears friendship bracelets, like Swifties do, and at each stop answers a surprise question about one of her older books (like Swift’s surprise songs). “Hollow Bones” follows Molly Fitzgerald, whose mother disappeared on 9/11, 25 years ago. Longtime fans get a hidden treat: Molly’s husband, Jesse, is a character from Picoult’s famous novel “My Sister’s Keeper.”
stories.why_it_matters: Authors now compete with streaming, TikTok and concerts for attention. Picoult is borrowing pop-star tricks to turn a book tour into a fan event and get readers to rediscover her backlist.
stories.camps: Fans: it is fun, generous and celebrates readers. Skeptics: big-name authors get these flashy tours and marketing money, while most writers, especially new ones, get little support.
stories.image_alt: Jodi Picoult in her book-covered white gown beside the cover of “Hollow Bones” and Taylor Swift in her “Tortured Poets” dress

terms.explain: When an author travels to bookstores and theaters to read, talk and sign books.
Taylor Swift’s record-breaking concert tour that covered songs from her whole career.
A hidden surprise or clue for fans to find.

stories.headline: The number of people in deep, many-sided poverty rises for the first time in 15 years, to 1.2 billion
stories.dek: More than half are children; most live in rural Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, UN report says.
stories.caveman: Being poor is not just about low income. The UN’s “Multidimensional Poverty Index” checks 10 things, like enough food, child deaths, years in school, and access to electricity, clean water and toilets. If you lack at least one-third of them, you count as “multidimensionally poor.” The 2026 update from the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and Oxford University covers 108 countries. It found 1.2 billion people living this way, 51.5 million more than last year, the first rise since the index started in 2010. About 617 million of them are children, and 83% live in the countryside. “The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP chief Alexander De Croo. Part of the increase comes from population growth, and many countries have old data, but some countries, like Egypt, Nepal and Tajikistan, cut poverty a lot.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the clearest sign in years that progress against global poverty is going backward, as wars, climate disasters and aid cuts pile up.
stories.camps: UN view: poverty is “unacceptable” and governments must invest in schools, health and basic services. A more cautious read: population growth and gaps in data affect the numbers, and 33 countries have still halved poverty since 2010, so progress is possible.

stories.headline: Philippine House votes to bar children under 13 from social media; the Senate wants a ban up to 18
stories.dek: The bill passed 287–3 after a string of school attacks that officials link to online content; the two chambers must now agree.
stories.caveman: On Monday, the Philippine House of Representatives passed a bill, 287 votes to 3, to keep young children off social media. Under the House version, children under about 13 could not create social media or interactive online-gaming accounts. Teens up to 17 could use them only with parents’ consent, and platforms could not show them targeted ads, endless-scroll algorithm feeds or livestreaming, or let them make online purchases or use “gambling-like” game features. The Senate already passed a stricter version that bans social media for everyone under 18. Now negotiators from both chambers must agree on one bill, and President Marcos must sign it. Officials say the push follows school shootings and stabbings they believe were influenced by online content.
stories.why_it_matters: Countries like Australia, Malaysia and Greece are also setting age limits for social media. How to protect kids online, without cutting them off from friends and information, is a question for parents everywhere, including Taiwan.
stories.camps: Supporters: social media and gaming can harm kids’ mental health and expose them to strangers and violent content; companies should be forced to protect them. Critics: bans are hard to enforce, age checks can threaten privacy, and kids may move to less safe corners of the internet.

stories.headline: France’s high school protests enter a fourth week as Macron calls for “respect”
stories.dek: About 130 of 3,700 high schools stayed closed Monday; officials say closures are falling but violence is rising.
stories.caveman: Since late September, French high school students (ages 15 to 18) have blocked the entrances of hundreds of high schools, called lycées, to protest bad classroom conditions, such as crowded classes, teacher shortages and run-down buildings. Riot police have been sent in, and some clashes have turned violent; injuries to students have put police tactics in the spotlight. On Monday, about 130 of France’s 3,700 lycées were still closed. The education ministry said eight school staff were hurt early Monday, mostly around Paris, Bordeaux and Lyon. President Emmanuel Macron said the students’ complaints “deserve time, consultations, discussion, and respect,” and urged calm. New nationwide protests were planned for Tuesday, pushed by the far-left party France Unbowed, followed by bigger cost-of-living protests on Saturday.
stories.why_it_matters: When teenagers walk out of school in large numbers, it shows deep anger about public services and the future. It is also becoming a big issue before France’s next presidential election.
stories.camps: Students and supporters: schools are falling apart and young people are not being heard. Government: the problems are real but need time and dialogue, and violence against staff is unacceptable. Critics of the left: some say France Unbowed is using students for political gain.

stories.headline: Indonesia’s forest fires choke Singapore and Malaysia with haze; President Prabowo orders tougher action
stories.dek: A very strong El Niño has made this an unusually bad fire season; flights and schools have been disrupted.
stories.caveman: Every dry season, forest and land fires burn in Indonesia, often set to clear land for farms and plantations. This year a very strong El Niño weather pattern has made it extra hot and dry, so the fires are unusually bad. Thick smoke, called haze, has blown into Singapore and Malaysia, darkening skies, disrupting flights, closing schools in Malaysia and raising health worries. On Oct. 12, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto chaired a meeting at the presidential palace and ordered officials to step up firefighting, especially in Central Kalimantan (on Borneo) and South Sumatra. Malaysia has offered planes, helicopters and firefighters, but officials said foreign help was not discussed. Indonesia also said it will not declare a national disaster for now because it can still handle the fires.
stories.why_it_matters: Haze crosses borders. Breathing smoky air is dangerous for children, old people and anyone with asthma or heart disease, and the fires also release huge amounts of planet-warming gas.
stories.camps: Indonesia’s government: it is doing its best and can handle the fires itself. Neighbors: Malaysia and Singapore want faster action and say companies linked to the fires should be held responsible. Environmental groups: the long-term fix is stopping land clearing and protecting forests.
